title: How to Care for Sarees So They Last for Years
description: A care routine for every fabric: what to do after each wear, how to wash cotton, how to store chiffon and organza, and the habits that make sarees last.

body.text: Three habits do most of the work, whatever the fabric. Air a saree before you put it away, instead of folding it straight after wearing. Store it wrapped in cotton and never in plastic. Take everything out two or three times a year and refold along different lines. Almost every saree that fails in storage failed for want of one of those three.
The rest is [fabric specific](/journal/indian-saree-fabrics-and-weaves), and it matters, because a cotton saree wants the opposite treatment from an organza one.
What should you do right after wearing a saree?
This is the part everyone skips, and it does more damage than any storage mistake.

A saree that has been worn has picked up perspiration, perfume and body oils, none of which are visible. Folded away immediately, they stay pressed into the fibres for months. Over time that produces yellowing along the folds, weakens the fabric, and attracts silverfish and moths, which are drawn to body residue more than to the cloth itself.
So hang it or lay it out somewhere shaded and airy for a few hours before folding. If it was a long day or a warm one, send it to be cleaned before storing, not after.
Why should you never store a saree dirty?

Related, and worth stating on its own because it is the single most expensive mistake people make. A stain you cannot see today will be a permanent brown mark in two years. Sugar, fruit juice and perspiration all oxidise slowly in storage and darken.
If something has happened to a saree, deal with it before it goes in the cupboard, not when you next want to wear it.
How do you care for each saree fabric?
Silk

Fold flat, never hang, wrap in muslin, dry clean only, and refold along different lines every few months. Silk has enough to say that it has [its own guide](/journal/how-to-care-for-silk-sarees), which covers zari, storage and cleaning in full.
The one rule to carry over here: water marks silk. Never dab a spill with a wet cloth, because you will trade a small stain for a large ring.
Handloom cotton
Cotton is the one fabric you can genuinely look after at home.

**The first wash matters most.** Handloom cottons often bleed on their first wash. Soak the saree alone in cold water with a generous handful of rock salt for about half an hour before washing. This helps set the dye. Wash it separately for the first two or three washes regardless.
**After that,** use cold water, a mild detergent and your hands, not a machine. Do not wring it. Press the water out and hang it to drip.
**Dry in shade.** Direct sun fades handloom dyes quickly and unevenly.
**Iron while slightly damp,** which gets the creases out without a fight.

**Go easy on starch.** A light starch gives a cotton saree its crispness, but heavily starched cotton stored for months attracts silverfish, which feed on the starch. Starch what you are about to wear, not what you are about to store.
Chiffon
Chiffon is light, unstable and stretches out of shape more easily than anything else in the wardrobe.
**Never hang it long term.** Its own weight will pull it out of true, and the drape will never sit the same way again.
**Roll it instead of folding it.** Around a cardboard tube or a rolled towel is ideal. Hard folds leave lines in chiffon that do not come out.
**Silk chiffon is dry clean only.** Synthetic chiffon can be hand washed cold, very gently, and never wrung.
**Iron on the lowest setting with a cotton cloth between the iron and the saree.** Direct heat will melt synthetic chiffon in seconds.

body.text: Georgette
Sturdier than chiffon and more forgiving. It holds a pleat, resists creasing, and tolerates short periods on a hanger.
Still store it folded loosely or rolled for anything longer than a few weeks. Cool iron, cloth in between, same as chiffon.
Organza
Organza is crisp, not fluid, and that is exactly the problem. It takes a crease and keeps it, sometimes permanently.
**Store flat or rolled, never folded hard.** Layer acid free tissue between the folds if you have no choice.
**Steam instead of ironing** where you can. If you must iron, use the lowest heat with a cloth in between and keep moving.
Silk organza softens and improves with wearing. Synthetic organza does not, so treat it more carefully.
Linen
Linen creases, and that is its character, not a fault. Store it folded, iron it damp if you want it smooth, and accept that it will not stay that way through an evening.
How do you protect zari on any saree?
Real zari is metal, so it tarnishes with moisture, perfume, deodorant and perspiration.

Let perfume and deodorant dry completely before you drape. Wrap sections heavy with zari in soft muslin or acid free tissue so the metallic work is not rubbing against the fabric beside it. Keep the storage area dry, with a silica gel sachet nearby but not touching the cloth.
And never run an iron directly over zari. Always a cloth in between, or the metal dulls and can lift away from the weave.
How do you remove a stain from a saree?
Blot, do not rub. Rubbing pushes a stain deeper into the weave and can lift the dye at the same time.
Work from the outside of the mark inwards, so you are not spreading it wider.
Do not use water on silk. Do not use hot water on anything, because heat sets protein stains permanently.

And resist household remedies on anything valuable. Lemon, vinegar, salt and toothpaste all appear in advice online and all of them can strip dye or damage zari. Take a good saree to someone who handles textiles for a living.
How should you pack sarees for travel?
Roll, do not fold. Rolled sarees arrive with soft waves that hang out in an hour, where folded ones arrive with hard lines you will be ironing in a hotel room.
Put the heaviest at the bottom of the case and the sheerest on top. Keep zari pieces in their own cloth bag so nothing snags on them.
What should you do when a preloved saree arrives?
Do three things before it goes into the cupboard.
**Air it** for a few hours, however carefully it was packed.
**Look at where the folds have been sitting.** Then refold it somewhere different. A saree that has been folded the same way for years needs its stress lines moved.

**Resist the urge to restore it.** Age in a textile is not damage. Softened silk, gently darkened zari and a slightly relaxed drape are what a saree of that age should look like, and aggressive cleaning takes those away permanently.
What does a yearly saree care routine look like?

**Twice or three times a year.** Take everything out. Let it air in the shade for a few hours. Refold along different lines. Check for insects and damp. This is the appointment that matters and it takes an afternoon.
**Every wear.** Air before folding. Clean before storing if the day was long.

**Once a year.** Check the falls and the pico edging on the sarees you wear often. These are sacrificial, meant to take the wear so the saree does not, and replacing a worn fall costs very little compared with the damage it prevents.
What shortens a saree's life fastest?

In order. Storing it dirty. Plastic covers. Hanging heavy silk for months. Leaving it folded the same way for years. Direct sunlight. Naphthalene balls, which stain and leave an odour that takes months to lift. Water on silk.
Every one of those is avoidable in under ten minutes.
